AIR-CIS: correspondence importance sampling against MTPFN, A-only and the exact oracle¶

Description¶

Written before the first run (2026-11-04). Spec and pre-registration: research_log/entries/2026-11-04_air-cis.md (the spec verbatim, then a pre-run addendum with deviations D1–D7). Issue #22.

Question. Is a scarce target task A predicted better by explicit inference of how it relates to a dense source B, than by an amortised in-context learner that sees both tasks (MTPFN)? Where does each lie between the A-only lower bound and the exact Bayes oracle, and which part of the remaining gap is the proposal's and which the decoder's?

The task (d = 1). B: 128 noisy points of a random function g. A: 1–10 noisy points of f_A(x) = h(g(T(x))), with an unknown monotone transform T of the input and an unknown output map h (identity or affine). The learner must predict A at 32 held-out queries.

The prior, without boundary leak.

  • g: a random tanh network with a sampled architecture (depth 1–3, width 16/32/64), mapped to [0, 1] by one global ECDF.
  • T(x) = c + w · Φ_θ(x): a smooth monotone flow Φ_θ of complexity J ∈ {0, 2, 4, 8, 16} (p = 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.15, 0.15) with a random amplitude s_T, followed by a random window (w ∈ [0.5, 1], c ∈ [0, 1 − w]). Why the window: Φ_θ alone fixes both ends of the box, so with h = id B would reveal A's values at x = 0 and x = 1 exactly, and at J = 0 everywhere. A Bayes learner exploits that, and it made the predictive in notebooks 15–16 artificially sharp at the edges. With the window, A's box maps into a random sub-interval of B's, and no value of A is known from B alone.
  • h = id with probability 0.5, else a + b·v with b ∈ [0.3, 1], a ∈ [0, 1 − b]. Noise σ_A, σ_B ∈ [0.005, 0.03]. Always related (no unrelated B in this stage).

The idea: CIS (correspondence importance sampling). The posterior over T is hard because it is discrete at heart: g is not monotone, so an A point with value y_a could sit on any of the branches of g where g ≈ y_a. A smooth proposal (AIR's flow) blurs these branches together. CIS proposes them explicitly:

  1. B surrogate. A GP on B gives μ_B(u), σ_B(u) (proposal only).
  2. Claims. Every A point claims a set of candidate locations u in B (the 16 best-matching B points by N(y_a; μ_B(u), …) times a prior table π(u | x_a), plus the 4 most likely under the prior).
  3. Coherent assignments by FFBS. Along A sorted by x, a hidden-Markov chain over the candidates with a soft monotone, smooth transition kernel (from the prior's stretch statistics); forward filtering, backward sampling draws whole assignments c, each with its exact probability q(c).
  4. A transform per assignment. For each sampled c, and each J (and each h type), Gauss–Newton fits the transform to "T(x_a) lands on c_a" and to A's values through μ_B; a Laplace Gaussian around the fit is the proposal for θ, and the Laplace evidence gives q(J | c).
  5. Exact weights. θ is drawn from the Laplace mixture (plus 10 % prior), and the importance weight uses the transported decoder D's likelihood p̂(A | B, θ), with an auxiliary term r(c | θ) that keeps the target exactly the posterior over (J, θ). The prediction is the weighted mixture of D's predictives.
  6. Rounds (U). Two cheap rounds with GP-surrogate weights reshape the location prior (a KDE of where the weighted transforms send each A point) and add local candidates; only the last round, with decoder weights, enters the estimate. The proposal can be wrong without biasing the result: errors cost effective sample size.

The decoder D is AIR's transported PFN: it predicts A from A's points and B moved into A's frame by T⁻¹, with a new feature log (T⁻¹)′(x_b) (how much the transform stretches B there), retrained on this prior.

Setup. Identical 256 evaluation tasks per n_A ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 10} (CPU-drawn, fixed seed) for every method:

  • A-only: a PFN with MTPFN's architecture trained on A alone (the clean lower bound); D's null head also shown.
  • MTPFN: #20's architecture (1.8 M parameters) trained on this prior, A and B as two tasks.
  • CIS-U: R = 1 and R = 3 rounds, K ∈ {32, 128} final samples.
  • IS-ref: prior importance sampling with K = 8192 and the same decoder: what CIS would reach with a perfect proposal.
  • Teacher: D at the true transform: the decoder's best case.
  • Oracle: the exact posterior predictive given the true g and σ_A (h integrated analytically; T's latents by tempered SMC per J, J mixed by the SMC evidence). An upper bound no method can beat in expectation. All trained components: seed 0 in this stage.

What to look for, and why.

  1. The ladder (the main figure): NLL against n_A for A-only, MTPFN, CIS, IS-ref, teacher, oracle, and the share of the A-only → oracle gap each closes. Answers "where does each method lie".
  2. Paired CIS − MTPFN per n_A with bootstrap CIs, overall and by stratum (J, number of extrema of g, true h). CIS should win where the posterior is multimodal (many extrema, high J, small n_A) and may lose nothing elsewhere.
  3. Decomposition of CIS's gap: proposal (CIS − IS-ref) vs decoder (IS-ref − oracle). In #21 (J = 2, AIR prior) proposals were within 0.02 nats of IS-ref and the decoder cost 0.11–0.16 nats; if that holds here, the next step is the decoder, not the proposal.
  4. Proposal diagnostics: ESS/K, branch hit rate and q-mass on the true branch combination by extrema stratum, R = 1 vs 3, K = 32 vs 128; the J posterior against the oracle's p(J | A, B) (calibration).
  5. Calibration of the predictive (PIT histograms, 50/90 % interval coverage) of MTPFN, CIS and the oracle: is a sharp predictive earned?
  6. Leak audit: the oracle's gain over A-only by the distance of x* to the boundary (h = id). A flat profile means B does not reveal A's edge values.
  7. Negative transfer: the share of tasks where each method is worse than A-only. Runtime per task.

GO / NO-GO (this notebook's comparison; the spec's C1, C3–C6 are evaluated as written, C2/C7/C8 are out of stage 1). GO: CIS-U (R = 3, K = 128) beats MTPFN by ≥ 0.05 nats with a paired 95 % CI excluding 0 at ≥ 2 of n_A ∈ {2, 3, 5}, and is not significantly worse at any n_A. NO-GO: CIS is significantly better at none of n_A ∈ {2, 3, 5}. Otherwise INCONCLUSIVE.

Limits. d = 1 only; always related (no unrelated-source stratum, so negative transfer is only tested within the related prior); h is identity or affine (no non-monotone h); one seed per trained model; the oracle knows g exactly (B is dense but noisy for every learner), so its gap is a bound, not a target; the decoder and MTPFN are trained on the same prior, so prior mismatch does not enter the comparison.

1. Oracle quality¶

The oracle's MC error per task: the mean over queries of |half 1 − half 2| of its log predictive density (two independent SMC runs of 1024 particles per J). This is about √2 × the standard error of one half; the reported oracle averages both halves.

How to read. The oracle is our upper reference, so its own noise must be small against the differences we interpret. For each task the table takes the mean over the 32 queries of |log p̂₁ − log p̂₂|, where p̂₁ and p̂₂ are two independent SMC estimates of the oracle's predictive density. Rows are n_A.

Here. The mean is 0.014–0.020 nats per task, the 95th percentile ≤ 0.05, and a few tasks reach 0.12–0.24. Averaged over 256 tasks, the oracle's error in a cell mean is about 0.02 / √256 ≈ 0.001 nats, far below every gap discussed below. Single-task oracle numbers (the examples) carry about ±0.02.

2. The ladder: A-only ≥ … ≥ oracle¶

The NLL per held-out query of A (mean over the 256 tasks; ± is the SE over tasks). Share = (A-only − method) / (A-only − oracle).

How to read.

  • Table: the mean NLL per held-out query of A (lower is better; nats per query, on the bar distribution's density scale, so values below 0 are normal), ± the SE over the 256 tasks.
  • Left plot: the same as lines. A-only (no transfer) is the top dashed line; the oracle (exact Bayes with the true g) is the bottom dashed line.
  • Right plot: each method's position between the two as a percentage. 0 % = no better than A-only; 100 % = as good as the oracle; above 100 % = better than the oracle, which is possible only with information the oracle lacks.
  • The SEs are over tasks and largely shared between methods (the same tasks), so paired differences (§3) are much more precise than the ± here suggest.

Here.

  • Every learner sits well below A-only, so B helps a lot. At n_A = 1 the gain over A-only is 0.50 (MTPFN) to 0.53 (CIS) nats per query.
  • The order is the same at every n_A: A-only ≈ null head > MTPFN > CIS > IS-ref ≥ CIS (exact likelihood) > oracle (IS-ref and exact CIS tie at n_A = 10). The teacher sits below the oracle.
  • The shares fall with n_A for every method. With more A data, A-only gets better on its own, and what remains to gain needs precise registration. MTPFN loses the most: 80 % → 39 %, against CIS 85 % → 54 %.
  • The teacher (decoder + true θ, J) is above 100 %: it is told the true transform, which the oracle must infer. It is a reference for the decoder, not a bound on any learner.
  • The decoder's null head equals the separately trained A-only PFN (within 0.02). The decoder's A-only part is as good as a dedicated model, so its gains are transfer, not a better A-model.

Examples: prior draws and the CIS predictive on a grid¶

How the figures are made (as notebooks 10, 13 and 15 draw their PPD heatmaps).

  • Top: a prior draw. B's function g with its 128 noisy points (left); A's truth f_A with its 10 points (right), numbered in the order they enter the context.
  • Bottom: the full CIS model (GP surrogate on B, claims + FFBS, per-assignment fits, decoder weights; R = 3, K = 128) predicts its bar distribution (400 bins) on a regular grid of 151 points in A's input space, at n_A = 1, 3, 10.
  • How to read a heatmap: each column x is the predictive density p(y | x, A, B), scaled to its own maximum. Dark means likely relative to the rest of that column; a single dark band is a confident prediction, several bands are a multimodal one.
  • Overlaid: the true f_A (orange) and the MAP function (green, dashed). The MAP function is the highest-weight importance sample's (J, θ) applied to B's GP mean, μ_B(T_θ̂(x)), with h by clipped least squares on A's points (identity if that is no worse). It is one sample, a summary, not the predictive.
  • Titles: the NLL on the task's 32 held-out test queries, from this live re-run and from the evaluation run. CIS is Monte Carlo, so they differ slightly. The corner gives the MAP sample's J and its normalised weight.
  • Task choice (fixed rule): J ≥ 2, at least 2 extrema of g and a range of g ≥ 0.4, so that there is structure to register. Among those, the task with the median CIS − MTPFN gap at n_A = 3, once for h = id and once for affine h. The first rule, ≥ 1 extremum, picked a nearly flat task. The y-axis is zoomed to the data.
  • Provenance: computed live on the CPU from the seed-0 decoder in runs/air_cis/, on the evaluation tasks (drawn on the CPU, so identical to the run's).

import dataclasses

import torch
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

from meta_pfn.experimental.air.cis import bsurrogate as BS
from meta_pfn.experimental.air.cis import core as CO
from meta_pfn.experimental.air.cis import decoder as CD
from meta_pfn.experimental.air.cis import fit as FT
from meta_pfn.experimental.air.cis import prior as CP
from meta_pfn.experimental.air.decoder import N_BINS, Y_HI, Y_LO

tc = OmegaConf.load(ROOT / "src/meta_pfn/configs/task/air_cis.yaml")
DEC = CD.CisDecoder(D=tc.dm, layers=tc.layers, tfeat=True)
DEC.load_state_dict(torch.load(ROOT / "runs/air_cis/pilot_20261104-174531/0/tracking/artifacts/model.pt", map_location="cpu"))
DEC.eval()
TE = CP.eval_tasks(256, 777, "cpu")  # the evaluation tasks (prior draws; CPU generator, identical to the run's)
XG = torch.linspace(0, 1, 151)  # the regular test grid in A's input space
G = len(XG)
CEN = (torch.linspace(Y_LO, Y_HI, N_BINS + 1)[:-1] + (Y_HI - Y_LO) / N_BINS / 2).numpy()
CMAP = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("seq", ["#fcfcfb", "#cde2fb", "#86b6ef", "#2a78d6", "#184f95", "#0d366b"])
GV = TE.g(torch.linspace(0, 1, 400)[None].expand(256, -1))
JS = list(CP.J_VALUES)


def pick(hid):
    """Fixed rule: J >= 2, >= 2 extrema of g, range of g >= 0.4; the median CIS − MTPFN gap at n_A = 3 in the stratum."""
    z = P.loc[3].assign(d=lambda v: v[CIS] - v.mtpfn).join(tasks.set_index("task")[["h_id", "J", "n_ext"]])
    z["g_range"] = (GV.amax(1) - GV.amin(1)).numpy()[z.index]
    c = z[(z.h_id == hid) & (z.J >= 2) & (z.n_ext >= 2) & (z.g_range >= 0.4)]
    return int((c.d - c.d.median()).abs().idxmin()), len(c)


def cis(j, n, spec, seed):
    """CIS-U (R = 3, K = 128; GP surrogate, decoder target) for task j with its first n A points, predicting on the
    grid and on the task's 32 test queries in one run. -> dict(probs [G, bins], lp_test [32], map [G], log_z, J_map,
    w_map, pJ {J: weight})."""
    t0 = TE.sub(torch.tensor([j])).head(n)
    t = dataclasses.replace(t0, xq=torch.cat([XG[None], t0.xq], 1), yq=torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, G), t0.yq], 1),
                            fq=torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, G), t0.fq], 1))  # fmt: skip
    gp = BS.fit(t.xb, t.yb)
    out = CO.run(t, gp, CO.DecoderTarget(DEC, t, n_perm=tc.n_perm), spec, R=3, K=128,
                 g=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed), full=True)  # fmt: skip
    W = out["W"][0].detach()
    k = int(W.argmax())  # the highest-weight sample: the MAP of the weighted posterior over (J, θ)
    lat, J = out["lat"][0, k][None], out["J"][0, k][None]
    m = lambda x: gp.mu(CP.transform(x, lat, J)).detach()  # noqa: E731  B's GP mean through the MAP transform
    a, b = 0.0, 1.0
    if n >= 2:  # h: least squares of y_A on m(x_A), inside the prior's support; identity if that is no worse
        ma, ya = m(t.xa)[0], t.ya[0]
        a_, b_ = torch.linalg.lstsq(torch.stack([torch.ones_like(ma), ma], 1), ya[:, None]).solution[:, 0].tolist()
        b_ = min(max(b_, CP.B_LO), 1.0)
        a_ = min(max(a_, 0.0), 1 - b_)
        if ((ya - a_ - b_ * ma) ** 2).sum() < ((ya - ma) ** 2).sum():
            a, b = a_, b_
    return {"probs": out["probs"][0, :G].detach().numpy(), "lp_test": out["lp"][0, G:].detach().numpy(),
            "map": (a + b * m(XG[None])[0]).numpy(), "log_z": float(out["log_z1"][0]), "J_map": int(J), "w_map": float(W[k]),
            "pJ": {Jv: float(W[out["J"][0] == Jv].sum()) for Jv in JS}}  # fmt: skip


def ylim_for(j):
    tj = TE.sub(torch.tensor([j]))
    lo, hi = min(float(GV[j].min()), float(tj.ya.min())), max(float(GV[j].max()), float(tj.ya.max()))
    return lo - 0.1 * (hi - lo), hi + 0.1 * (hi - lo)


def heat(ax, pr, j, n, YL, fmap=None):
    tj = TE.sub(torch.tensor([j]))
    ax.imshow((pr / pr.max(1, keepdims=True)).T, origin="lower", aspect="auto", extent=[0, 1, Y_LO, Y_HI], cmap=CMAP,
              vmin=0, vmax=1, interpolation="nearest")  # fmt: skip
    ax.plot(XG, tj.f_a(XG[None])[0], color=C[1], lw=1.4, label="true f_A")
    if fmap is not None:
        ax.plot(XG, fmap, color=C[2], lw=1.4, ls="--", label="MAP function")
    ax.scatter(tj.xa[0, :n], tj.ya[0, :n], s=22, color=INK, edgecolor="white", lw=0.7, zorder=3, label="A points used")
    ax.set(ylim=YL, xlim=(0, 1))
    ax.grid(False)


def task_panels(axb, axa, j, YL):
    tj, info = TE.sub(torch.tensor([j])), tasks.set_index("task").loc[j]
    ug = torch.linspace(0, 1, 400)
    axb.plot(ug, TE.g.at(torch.tensor([j]))(ug[None])[0], color=INK, lw=1.5, label="g (B's function)")
    axb.scatter(tj.xb[0], tj.yb[0], s=9, color=C[3], zorder=3, label="B data (128 points)")
    axb.set(xlabel="u (B's input)", ylabel="y", ylim=YL)
    axb.set_title(f"Task {j} (a prior draw): the dense source B", loc="left", fontsize=10)
    axb.legend(fontsize=8)
    axa.plot(XG, tj.f_a(XG[None])[0], color=C[1], lw=1.8, label="f_A (truth)")
    axa.plot(XG, TE.g.at(torch.tensor([j]))(XG[None])[0], color=INK, lw=1, ls=":", label="g at the same x (no warp)")
    axa.scatter(tj.xa[0], tj.ya[0], s=22, color=INK, zorder=3, label="A data (10 points; the first n_A are used)")
    for i in range(tj.xa.shape[1]):
        axa.annotate(str(i + 1), (float(tj.xa[0, i]), float(tj.ya[0, i])), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(4, 4),
                     fontsize=7, color=MUTED)  # fmt: skip
    hs = "h = id" if info.h_id else f"h affine (a = {info.a:.2f}, b = {info.b:.2f})"
    axa.set(xlabel="x (A's input)", ylabel="y", ylim=YL)
    axa.set_title(f"The scarce target A: J = {info.J}, {info.n_ext} extrema of g, {hs}, σ_A = {info.sig_a:.3f}",
                  loc="left", fontsize=10)  # fmt: skip
    axa.legend(fontsize=8)


def example(j):
    YL = ylim_for(j)
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(15, 8.2))
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 6)
    task_panels(fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :3]), fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 3:]), j, YL)
    for c_, n in enumerate((1, 3, 10)):
        r = cis(j, n, FT.Spec(), seed=100 + n)
        ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2 * c_ : 2 * c_ + 2])
        heat(ax, r["probs"], j, n, YL, r["map"])
        nl = float(nll[(nll.task == j) & (nll.n_a == n) & (nll.method == CIS)].nll.iloc[0])
        ax.set_title(f"CIS bar-distribution PPD, n_A = {n}: NLL {-r['lp_test'].mean():.2f} here, {nl:.2f} in the run",
                     loc="left", fontsize=9)  # fmt: skip
        ax.text(0.99, 0.03, f"MAP: J = {r['J_map']}, weight {r['w_map']:.2f}", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right",
                fontsize=8, color=MUTED)  # fmt: skip
        ax.set_xlabel("x (A's input, regular test grid)")
        if c_ == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel("y (each column scaled to its max)")
            ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


def jgrid(j, NA=(1, 2, 3, 5, 10)):
    """Rows: the CIS predictive with J fixed (spec js = (J,)), then the mixture over J; columns: n_A.
    p(J | A, B) ∝ p(J) Ẑ_J with Ẑ_J the J-conditional run's evidence estimate; the mixture is Σ_J p(J | A, B) PPD_J."""
    YL, info = ylim_for(j), tasks.set_index("task").loc[j]
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(len(JS) + 1, len(NA), figsize=(3.2 * len(NA), 2.25 * (len(JS) + 1)), sharex=True,
                            sharey=True, squeeze=False)  # fmt: skip
    rows = []
    for c_, n in enumerate(NA):
        res = {Jv: cis(j, n, FT.Spec(js=(Jv,), pj=(1.0,)), seed=1000 * Jv + n) for Jv in JS}
        lw = np.array([np.log(p_) + res[Jv]["log_z"] for Jv, p_ in zip(JS, CP.P_J, strict=True)])
        w = np.exp(lw - lw.max())
        w /= w.sum()
        for r_, Jv in enumerate(JS):
            ax, rr = axs[r_, c_], res[Jv]
            heat(ax, rr["probs"], j, n, YL, rr["map"])
            nlJ = -rr["lp_test"].mean()
            ax.set_title(f"n_A={n}, J={Jv}: p(J|A)={w[r_]:.2f}, NLL {nlJ:.2f}", loc="left", fontsize=8,
                         fontweight="bold" if Jv == info.J else "normal")  # fmt: skip
            rows.append({"n_A": n, "J": Jv, "p(J | A, B)": w[r_], "NLL (J fixed)": nlJ})
        mix = sum(w[r_] * res[Jv]["probs"] for r_, Jv in enumerate(JS))
        lp_mix = np.log(sum(w[r_] * np.exp(res[Jv]["lp_test"]) for r_, Jv in enumerate(JS)))
        heat(axs[-1, c_], mix, j, n, YL)
        nl = float(nll[(nll.task == j) & (nll.n_a == n) & (nll.method == CIS)].nll.iloc[0])
        axs[-1, c_].set_title(f"n_A={n}, mixture: NLL {-lp_mix.mean():.2f} (run {nl:.2f})", loc="left", fontsize=8)
        rows.append({"n_A": n, "J": "mixture", "p(J | A, B)": 1.0, "NLL (J fixed)": -lp_mix.mean()})
    for r_, Jv in enumerate(JS):
        axs[r_, 0].set_ylabel(f"J = {Jv}" + (" (true)" if Jv == info.J else ""), fontsize=9)
    axs[-1, 0].set_ylabel("mixture over J", fontsize=9)
    axs[0, 0].legend(fontsize=6, loc="upper left")
    for ax in axs[-1]:
        ax.set_xlabel("x (A's input)")
    fig.suptitle(f"Task {j}: the CIS predictive per complexity J (rows) against n_A (columns); bold title = the true J "
                 f"({info.J}). Weight = p(J | A, B); NLL on the task's 32 test queries.", x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=10)  # fmt: skip
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    display(tab.pivot_table(index="J", columns="n_A", values="p(J | A, B)", sort=False).round(2).rename_axis("p(J | A, B)"))
    display(tab.pivot_table(index="J", columns="n_A", values="NLL (J fixed)", sort=False).round(2).rename_axis("NLL"))


T_ID, n_id = pick(True)
T_AFF, n_aff = pick(False)
print(f"examples (fixed rule): h = id task {T_ID} (of {n_id} candidates), h affine task {T_AFF} (of {n_aff})")

examples (fixed rule): h = id task 194 (of 5 candidates), h affine task 88 (of 3)

Example 1: h = id¶

In [5]:
example(T_ID)

Here (task 194, h = id, true J = 2).

  • The task: g has a plateau at 0.5, a peak at 0.73 near u = 0.6 and a drop to 0.2. The warp moves the peak to x ≈ 0.93 in A, and A's first point lies on the plateau.
  • n_A = 1: one point on the plateau cannot locate the peak. The predictive keeps the plateau and spreads its mass over two readings of the right end: a rise to the peak, or the drop to 0.2. The MAP sample (weight 0.08) is only one of many and is misleading on its own.
  • n_A = 3: the third point sits on the peak (x = 0.89). The predictive commits to the rise and also predicts the sharp drop past x ≈ 0.95, which no A point shows: that comes from B through the registration.
  • n_A = 10: a narrow band around f_A, with the MAP function close to the truth.
  • NLL on this task (run, n_A = 1 / 3 / 10):
    • A-only −0.81 / −0.88 / −1.60;
    • MTPFN −0.95 / −1.51 / −1.52;
    • CIS −1.45 / −1.50 / −1.91;
    • oracle −1.42 / −1.78 / −1.96.
  • Monte Carlo noise: a single task's NLL varies by about 0.1–0.2 between CIS runs at K = 128 (compare the live and run values in the titles). Only the 256-task means are precise.

Example 2: affine h¶

In [6]:
example(T_AFF)

Here (task 88, affine h: a = 0.07, b = 0.31; true J = 2).

  • The task: f_A is g compressed to about a third of its range and shifted down. A's points cover x ≥ 0.33; the left part, where g falls steeply, has no A point.
  • n_A = 1: the predictive is already at the right level and scale. B fixes the shape, and the h posterior places it from one point.
  • The MAP function at n_A = 1 is drawn with h = identity, because h is not fitted from one point. Its level is therefore wrong, and it shows how much of the work h does.
  • n_A = 3 and 10: the predictive follows the dip-bump-dip structure. The left end stays uncertain at n_A = 10: the band fans out where no A point is, as it should.
  • NLL on this task (run, n_A = 1 / 3 / 10):
    • A-only −1.55 / −2.07 / −1.91;
    • MTPFN −2.02 / −2.16 / −2.10;
    • CIS −2.06 / −2.09 / −2.07;
    • oracle −2.07 / −2.18 / −2.22. With a compressed f_A, A alone already does well from n_A = 3. Here CIS is level with MTPFN, not better (this task was picked as the median of a stratum of 3).

The predictive per complexity J¶

The same two tasks, with CIS restricted to one J at a time.

  • Rows: J ∈ {0, 2, 4, 8, 16} (proposal and target prior on that J only).
  • Columns: n_A ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 10}.
  • Bottom row: their mixture with weights p(J | A, B) ∝ p(J) Ẑ_J. Here p(J) is the prior (0.2 / 0.3 / 0.2 / 0.15 / 0.15) and Ẑ_J is the J-conditional run's evidence estimate: the mean importance weight, i.e. the decoder's estimate of p(A | B, J).
  • Titles: the weight and the NLL of that J-conditional predictive on the task's 32 test queries. The true J's titles are bold.
  • Tables: the same numbers.

How to read it:

  • A row whose predictive already fits f_A but has a small weight means A's points cannot tell that J from the others. A large weight on a row with a bad NLL means the evidence is misled.
  • The mixture's NLL is never worse than the weighted average of the rows' log densities (it is a log-mean-exp).

Here.

Task 194 (h = id, true J = 2).

  • Weights: the weight on the true J rises with n_A, from 0.31 to 0.47. J = 0 drops from 0.24 to 0.06: once the peak and the drop are seen, a pure window shift (J = 0) cannot place them.
  • Each J's predictive: at n_A = 1 every row shows the same two hypotheses (rise or drop at the right end). They differ in how much mass they give each.
  • From n_A = 3: J = 2, 8 and 16 predict similarly well (NLL −1.59 to −1.74). J = 4 has a worse NLL (−1.29) despite a similar picture: one of its modes is narrower and misses some test points. These are differences of a single K = 128 run each.
  • The mixture is close to the best row from n_A = 5 on.

Task 88 (affine h, true J = 2).

  • The evidence picks the wrong J: at n_A = 10, J = 0 gets 0.65 and the true J = 2 only 0.23.
  • The NLLs say the opposite: J = 0's predictive is the worst (−1.96 against −2.12 for J = 2).
  • Why (plausibly; not checked): the evidence is computed only at A's 10 points, which J = 0 fits as well as J = 2, and with fewer free parameters an equally good fit gets more evidence. The test NLL also scores queries in the gaps, including the steep left part where A has no point, and there J = 0's predictive does worse. The pictures do not show where at this scale.
  • This is the over-confidence of §5 in one task: the J weights follow the fit at A's points, while the test NLL also depends on the extrapolation. The mixture (−2.04) is pulled towards the J = 0 row.
  • At n_A ≤ 3 the weights are close to the prior (0.2 / 0.3 / 0.2 / 0.15 / 0.15), and all rows predict about equally well: J is not identified yet.

In general:

  • J mostly matters where A has no points.
  • With few points, all J's agree near the data and differ in the gaps.
  • The posterior over J only sharpens when the data see the structure that separates them.
  • The oracle's weights would tell whether the decoder's evidence or the problem itself makes J hard to pin down (§5: mostly the latter, plus some decoder over-confidence).

3. The pre-registered comparison: CIS-U (R = 3, K = 128) against MTPFN¶

Paired over tasks: d = CIS − MTPFN per task (negative means CIS is better), with a 95 % bootstrap CI (10 000 resamples). GO: d ≤ −0.05 with the CI below 0 at ≥ 2 of n_A ∈ {2, 3, 5}, and CIS not significantly worse at any n_A. NO-GO: CIS significantly better at none of n_A ∈ {2, 3, 5}. Otherwise INCONCLUSIVE.

In [9]:
rows = []
for n in NS:
    d = (P.loc[n][CIS] - P.loc[n]["mtpfn"]).to_numpy()
    lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(d, n_boot=10_000)
    rows.append({"n_A": n, "CIS − MTPFN": d.mean(), "CI lo": lo, "CI hi": hi, "better": hi < 0, "worse": lo > 0,
                 "meets −0.05": (d.mean() <= -0.05) and hi < 0, "share of tasks CIS better": (d < 0).mean()})
V = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("n_A")
display(V.round(4))
key = V.loc[[n for n in (2, 3, 5) if n in V.index]]
n_go, any_worse, n_better = int(key["meets −0.05"].sum()), bool(V.worse.any()), int(key.better.sum())
verdict = "GO" if (n_go >= 2 and not any_worse) else ("NO-GO" if n_better == 0 else "INCONCLUSIVE")
print(f"cells meeting the GO margin (n_A in 2, 3, 5): {n_go}; significantly worse anywhere: {any_worse}; "
      f"significantly better (2, 3, 5): {n_better}  ->  proposed verdict: {verdict}")

How to read.

  • Columns:
    • "CIS − MTPFN": the mean paired difference in NLL (negative = CIS better);
    • "CI lo / hi": its 95 % bootstrap CI over tasks;
    • "better / worse": whether the CI excludes 0 on either side;
    • "meets −0.05": the pre-registered GO condition per cell;
    • "share of tasks CIS better": the fraction of tasks with a negative difference.
  • Verdict line: the rule applied to n_A ∈ {2, 3, 5}.

Here.

  • CIS is significantly better at every n_A, by 0.029–0.045 nats, and on 57–66 % of tasks.
  • The pre-registered GO margin of 0.05 is reached nowhere; the largest gap, 0.045 at n_A = 5, is close.
  • So the registered verdict is INCONCLUSIVE. The direction is consistent; the size is smaller than the margin set beforehand.
  • One training seed per learned part: seed variation could move these numbers by a few hundredths.

4. Where the error comes from¶

  • proposal error = CIS − IS-ref (the decoder held fixed);
  • decoder error = IS-ref − oracle (and teacher − oracle: the decoder with the true θ);
  • MTPFN's amortisation error = MTPFN − oracle;
  • proposal quality without the decoder = CIS (exact likelihood) − oracle.
In [10]:
dec = pd.DataFrame({"proposal: CIS − IS-ref": m[CIS] - m.isref, "decoder: IS-ref − oracle": m.isref - m.oracle,
                    "decoder: teacher − oracle": m.teacher - m.oracle, "MTPFN − oracle": m.mtpfn - m.oracle})
if "cis_exact_r3_k128" in m:
    dec["CIS exact − oracle"] = m["cis_exact_r3_k128"] - m.oracle
for k in [c for c in m.columns if c.startswith("cis_r")]:
    dec[f"{k} − IS-ref"] = m[k] - m.isref
display(dec.round(3))
proposal: CIS − IS-ref decoder: IS-ref − oracle decoder: teacher − oracle MTPFN − oracle CIS exact − oracle cis_r1_k128 − IS-ref cis_r1_k32 − IS-ref cis_r3_k128 − IS-ref cis_r3_k32 − IS-ref
n_a
1 0.009 0.088 -0.224 0.126 0.046 0.023 0.037 0.009 0.057
2 0.017 0.096 -0.173 0.143 0.040 0.013 0.058 0.017 0.046
3 0.016 0.094 -0.124 0.149 0.048 0.016 0.051 0.016 0.046
5 0.008 0.093 -0.072 0.146 0.051 0.020 0.032 0.008 0.029
8 0.013 0.083 -0.039 0.125 0.045 0.018 0.038 0.013 0.043
10 0.012 0.081 -0.017 0.122 0.080 0.015 0.030 0.012 0.024

How to read. Every column is a difference of mean NLLs. Positive means the first method is worse.

  • Proposal error (CIS − IS-ref): the same decoder, a better proposal. IS-ref uses 8192 prior samples, close to an exact posterior for that decoder.
  • Decoder error (IS-ref − oracle): IS-ref against exact Bayes with the true g. It contains the decoder's approximation of the likelihood and of the predictive, plus g being seen only through 128 noisy points.
  • Teacher − oracle: negative, because the teacher knows θ.
  • MTPFN − oracle: MTPFN's total (amortisation) error.
  • CIS exact − oracle: the proposal's error when the likelihood is exact. This is CIS's proposal on the oracle's own target with K = 128.
  • cis_rR_kK − IS-ref: the proposal error at each budget.

Here.

  • The proposal costs 0.008–0.017 nats at R = 3, K = 128, and 0.024–0.058 at K = 32.
  • The decoder costs 0.081–0.096 at every n_A: about 6 × the proposal error, and the main limit of the pipeline.
  • MTPFN's total error is 0.12–0.15.
  • With the exact likelihood, CIS's proposal is 0.04–0.05 from the oracle (0.08 at n_A = 10, where its SE is 0.05). That is larger than its error relative to IS-ref under the decoder: the exact likelihood is sharper, so importance sampling with 128 samples is harder.
  • Practical reading: improving the decoder is worth up to about 0.09 nats; improving the proposal at most about 0.015.

5. Proposal diagnostics (C1, C3–C6)¶

ESS/K of the final round, branch hit rate (at least one final-round sample has the true branch combination), the weight mass on the true branch combination, and the weight on the true J. Strata: extrema of g, h.

In [11]:
dg = diag[diag.method.str.startswith("cis")].merge(tasks[["task", "ext", "h", "J"]], on="task")
dg["ess_k"] = dg.ess / dg.K
g = dg.groupby(["method", "n_a"]).agg(ess_k=("ess_k", "median"), hit=("hit", "mean"), qmass=("qmass", "mean"),
                                    pJ_true=("pJ_true", "mean"), sec=("sec_per_task", "first"))
display(g.unstack("n_a").round(3))
print("C1: branch hit rate, U (R = 1, K = 128), by extrema stratum (pass: ≥ 0.95 at n_A ≥ 2 on every stratum)")
c1 = dg[dg.method == "cis_r1_k128"].pivot_table(index="ext", columns="n_a", values="hit", aggfunc="mean")
display(c1.round(3))
c1_pass = bool((c1[[n for n in c1.columns if n >= 2]] >= 0.95).all().all())
c3 = (m[CIS] - m.isref)[[n for n in NS if n >= 2]]
c3_pass = bool((c3 <= 0.03).all())
e = dg.groupby(["method", "n_a"]).ess.median().unstack("n_a")
c4 = (e.loc[CIS] / e.loc["cis_r1_k128"])
eh = dg[dg.h == "h affine"].groupby(["method", "n_a"]).ess.median().unstack("n_a")
c4h = eh.loc[CIS] / eh.loc["cis_r1_k128"]
c4_pass = bool((c4[[n for n in NS if n >= 5]] >= 1.5).all() and (c4h[[n for n in NS if n >= 3]] >= 1.5).all())
gap = m[CIS] - m.isref
c5_pass = bool(gap.loc[1] > gap[[n for n in NS if n >= 2]].max()) if 1 in gap.index else None
c6 = dg[(dg.method == CIS) & (dg.h == "h affine")].groupby("n_a").hit.mean()
c6_pass = bool((c6[[n for n in NS if n >= 3]] >= 0.9).all())
print(pd.DataFrame([
    ("C1 coverage: hit ≥ 0.95, R=1 K=128, n_A ≥ 2, every stratum (AIR-flow clause not evaluated, D4)", c1_pass),
    ("C3 accuracy: CIS − IS-ref ≤ 0.03 at n_A ≥ 2: " + " / ".join(f"{v:.3f}" for v in c3), c3_pass),
    ("C4 rounds: ESS(R=3)/ESS(R=1) ≥ 1.5 at n_A ≥ 5: " + " / ".join(f"{c4[n]:.2f}" for n in NS if n >= 5)
     + "; h affine at n_A ≥ 3: " + " / ".join(f"{c4h[n]:.2f}" for n in NS if n >= 3), c4_pass),
    ("C5 n_A = 1 hardest: gap at 1 vs max at ≥ 2: " + (f"{gap.loc[1]:.3f} vs {gap[[n for n in NS if n >= 2]].max():.3f}" if 1 in gap.index else "n/a"), c5_pass),
    ("C6 h: hit ≥ 0.9 under h affine at n_A ≥ 3: " + " / ".join(f"{c6[n]:.2f}" for n in NS if n >= 3), c6_pass),
], columns=["hypothesis", "pass"]).to_string(index=False))
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.8))
for i, k in enumerate(sorted(dg.method.unique())):

    axs[0].plot(range(len(z)), z.ess_k, marker="o", color=C[i % len(C)], label=k)

C4 rounds: ESS(R=3)/ESS(R=1) ≥ 1.5 at n_A ≥ 5: 1.02 / 1.01 / 1.10; h affine at n_A ≥ 3: 0.99 / 1.00 / 1.04 / 1.10 False
                                                       C5 n_A = 1 hardest: gap at 1 vs max at ≥ 2: 0.009 vs 0.017 False
                                             C6 h: hit ≥ 0.9 under h affine at n_A ≥ 3: 0.99 / 0.99 / 0.97 / 0.96  True

How to read.

  • Table: per method and n_A,
    • the median ESS / K of the final round (the effective share of the K weighted samples);
    • the branch hit rate (at least one final-round sample has the true branch combination, i.e. each A point is on the correct monotone segment of g);
    • the q-mass (weight) on the true branch combination;
    • the weight on the true J;
    • the wall time per task.
  • C1 table: the hit rate by number of extrema of g.
  • Hypothesis table: C1 and C3–C6 with their values.
  • Plots: the three diagnostics over n_A, one line per (R, K).

Here.

  • ESS / K falls from about 0.3 at n_A = 1 to 0.15–0.23 at n_A = 10: each A point sharpens the posterior and the proposal does not quite keep up. Still, 0.16 × 128 ≈ 20 effective samples at n_A = 10.
  • The branch hit rate is ≥ 0.96 for K = 128 everywhere. It drops only for ≥ 3 extrema at n_A ≥ 8 (0.85, 0.75 on 20 tasks): many points on a wiggly g give many possible branch combinations. This is the one C1 failure.
  • The rounds do not help (C4): R = 3 has the same ESS as R = 1. The round-1 proposal is already near the posterior for this decoder (proposal error ≤ 0.02), so there is little to refine.
  • C5: the gap at n_A = 1 is 0.009, not the largest. With one point the posterior is broad, which importance sampling handles easily.
  • The weight on the true J rises only from 0.21 to 0.26 (the prior alone would put 0.215 on the true J on average): J is weakly identified (§5, p(J)).

Calibration of p(J)¶

For the oracle and CIS: the mean posterior weight on each J, against the frequency of the true J among tasks whose posterior puts that much weight on it (binned reliability). On the prior, a calibrated p(J | A) is reliable.

In [12]:
oj = diag[diag.method == "oracle"].merge(tasks[["task", "J"]], on="task")
oj["is_true"] = oj.J_val == oj.J
rel = []
for src, z in (("oracle", oj[["n_a", "pJ", "is_true"]]),):
    z = z.assign(bin=pd.cut(z.pJ, np.linspace(0, 1, 6), include_lowest=True))
    rel.append(z.groupby(["n_a", "bin"], observed=True).agg(mean_p=("pJ", "mean"), freq=("is_true", "mean"), n=("pJ", "size")).assign(src=src))
cj = dg[dg.method == CIS]
long = pd.concat([cj[["n_a", f"pJ_{v}"]].rename(columns={f"pJ_{v}": "pJ"}).assign(is_true=(cj.J == v).values) for v in (0, 2, 4, 8, 16)])
long = long.assign(bin=pd.cut(long.pJ, np.linspace(0, 1, 6), include_lowest=True))
rel.append(long.groupby(["n_a", "bin"], observed=True).agg(mean_p=("pJ", "mean"), freq=("is_true", "mean"), n=("pJ", "size")).assign(src=CIS))
R = pd.concat(rel).reset_index()
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, src in zip(axs, ("oracle", CIS), strict=True):
    for i, n in enumerate(NS):
        z = R[(R.src == src) & (R.n_a == n)]
        ax.plot(z.mean_p, z.freq, marker="o", color=C[i % len(C)], label=f"n_A={n}")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color=MUTED, lw=1, ls=":")
    ax.set(xlabel="posterior weight on J", ylabel="frequency of the true J")
    ax.set_title(f"p(J) reliability: {src}", loc="left")
axs[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

How to read.

  • Reliability of the posterior over J: every (task, J) pair is a prediction "J has weight p", binned by p (x-axis) against the fraction of those pairs where J is the true one (y-axis).
  • On the diagonal = calibrated; above = under-confident; below = over-confident.
  • The oracle's p(J) comes from its SMC evidences (exact likelihood); CIS's from its weights (decoder likelihood).
  • Points beyond 0.5 rest on few tasks.

Here.

  • The oracle's p(J) is calibrated: on the diagonal where data are dense, and slightly under-confident above 0.5.
  • CIS is over-confident: when it puts 0.7–0.9 on one J, that J is mostly true only 30–55 % of the time (one n_A is higher, on few tasks).
  • With an exact likelihood, J is weakly identified (the oracle rarely exceeds 0.6). CIS's decoder evidence separates the J's more sharply than the data support. The J-grid figures above show this per task. It costs little NLL, because neighbouring J's often predict alike.

6. Predictive calibration¶

PIT = the predictive CDF at the held-out y. Coverage of the central 50 % / 90 % intervals = the share of PIT in [0.25, 0.75] / [0.05, 0.95].

In [13]:
MS = [k for k in ("aonly", "mtpfn", CIS, "oracle") if k in q.method.unique()]
cov = q[q.method.isin(MS)].assign(c50=lambda z: z.cdf.between(0.25, 0.75), c90=lambda z: z.cdf.between(0.05, 0.95))
display(cov.groupby(["method", "n_a"])[["c50", "c90"]].mean().unstack("n_a").round(3))
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, len(MS), figsize=(4 * len(MS), 3.2), sharey=True)
for ax, k in zip(axs, MS, strict=True):
    for i, n in enumerate((1, 3, 10)):
        z = q[(q.method == k) & (q.n_a == n)].cdf
        ax.hist(z, bins=20, range=(0, 1), density=True, histtype="step", color=C[i], lw=2, label=f"n_A={n}")
    ax.axhline(1, color=MUTED, lw=1, ls=":")
    ax.set(xlabel="PIT")
    ax.set_title(k, loc="left")
axs[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

How to read.

  • PIT: the predictive CDF evaluated at the held-out y. For a calibrated predictive it is uniform on [0, 1]: flat histograms at density 1 (dotted line).
  • A U-shape means too narrow, a hump too wide, a slope a biased location.
  • Table: the share of PIT inside [0.25, 0.75] (should be 0.5) and inside [0.05, 0.95] (should be 0.9).

Here.

  • Every method is close to calibrated: 50 % coverage 0.48–0.52, 90 % coverage 0.89–0.91.
  • The histograms are flat within noise, with small bumps in the outer bins:
    • A-only and CIS have a little excess at PIT ≈ 1 at n_A ≤ 3 (truth slightly above the predictive);
    • the oracle has some at PIT ≈ 0.
  • So the methods differ in sharpness, as the NLL shows, not in calibration. The gains are honest; they are not bought with over-confidence.

7. Leak audit (a validity check of the prior)¶

The oracle's gain over A-only by the distance of x* to the box boundary, h = id stratum. Flagged if, within 0.05 of the boundary, the gain exceeds 1.3 × the interior gain (notebook 16's leak gave 1.04 vs 0.61 nats, 1.7 ×).

In [14]:
qq = q[q.method.isin(["aonly", "oracle", "mtpfn", CIS])].pivot_table(index=["n_a", "task", "q"], columns="method", values="lp").reset_index()
qq = qq.merge(tasks[["task", "h_id"]], on="task").merge(q[q.method == "oracle"][["n_a", "task", "q", "x"]], on=["n_a", "task", "q"])
qq["dist"] = np.minimum(qq.x, 1 - qq.x)
qq["zone"] = np.where(qq.dist < 0.05, "edge (< 0.05)", "interior")
rows = []
for n in NS:
    z = qq[(qq.n_a == n) & qq.h_id]
    gains = {k: z.groupby("zone").apply(lambda v, k=k: (v[k] - v.aonly).mean()) for k in ("oracle", "mtpfn", CIS) if k in z}
    ratio = gains["oracle"]["edge (< 0.05)"] / gains["oracle"]["interior"]
    rows.append({"n_A": n, **{f"{k} gain {zz}": v[zz] for k, v in gains.items() for zz in v.index}, "oracle edge / interior": ratio,
                 "flag (> 1.3)": ratio > 1.3})
L = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("n_A")
display(L.round(3))
bins = np.linspace(0, 0.5, 11)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
for i, n in enumerate((2, 3, 5)):
    z = qq[(qq.n_a == n) & qq.h_id]
    b = pd.cut(z.dist, bins)
    gg = (z.oracle - z.aonly).groupby(b, observed=True).mean()
    ax.plot((bins[:-1] + bins[1:]) / 2, gg.values, marker="o", color=C[i], label=f"n_A={n}")
ax.set(xlabel="distance of x* to the boundary", ylabel="oracle gain over A-only (nats)")
ax.set_title("Leak audit, h = id", loc="left")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()

How to read.

  • The pre-registered check, h = id tasks. A leak like notebook 16's pinned f_A = g at the box ends, so the oracle would gain much more near the boundary.
  • Table: the mean gain over A-only (in nats; positive = better than A-only) of the oracle, MTPFN and CIS, for queries within 0.05 of the boundary ("edge") and the rest. The last columns are the oracle's edge / interior ratio and the pre-registered flag (> 1.3).
  • Plot: the oracle's gain against the distance to the boundary.

Here.

  • The flag is raised: the ratio is 1.32 at n_A = 1, rising to 2.26 at n_A = 10.
  • The gain falls smoothly with the distance to the boundary, over the whole range 0–0.25. It does not drop sharply just inside the edge, as a pinned end would make it.
  • The ratio grows with n_A because the interior gain shrinks faster (A's points fill the interior).
  • The §7b controls test this directly.

7b. Leak audit, post-hoc controls (added after the results; not pre-registered)¶

The pre-registered audit flags. Two controls separate a leak from A-only's weakness at the edge:

  1. Prior level: a leak in the prior would pin f_A to g at the ends. Notebook 16's leak gave 0.003 at the ends against 0.055 in the middle. Shown here: the mean |f_A − g| (h = id) by x, over 4000 prior tasks.
  2. Matched queries: edge queries are always outside A's hull, where A-only extrapolates from one side. Among queries outside A's hull, the edge gain is compared with the interior gain at a matched distance to the nearest A point (quartile bins, weighted by the edge queries' bin counts).
In [15]:
import torch

from meta_pfn.experimental.air.cis import prior as CP

tp = CP.sample_tasks(CP.CisCfg(), 4000, 1, torch.Generator().manual_seed(11))
xg = torch.linspace(0, 1, 101)[None].expand(4000, -1)
dd = (tp.f_a(xg) - tp.g(xg)).abs()[tp.hid]
print("prior |f_A − g|, h = id: x = 0: %.3f | x < 0.05: %.3f | 0.4–0.6: %.3f | x > 0.95: %.3f | x = 1: %.3f" % (
    dd[:, 0].mean(), dd[:, :5].mean(), dd[:, 40:61].mean(), dd[:, 96:].mean(), dd[:, -1].mean()))
TE = CP.eval_tasks(256, 777, "cpu")
xa = TE.xa.numpy()
assert np.allclose(TE.xq.numpy().reshape(-1), q[(q.method == "oracle") & (q.n_a == NS[0])].x.to_numpy(), atol=1e-6)
pp = qq[qq.h_id].copy()
pp["gain"], pp["edge"] = pp.oracle - pp.aonly, pp.dist < 0.05
pp["dA"] = [np.abs(xa[t, :n] - x).min() for t, n, x in zip(pp.task, pp.n_a, pp.x, strict=True)]
pp["out"] = [(x < xa[t, :n].min()) or (x > xa[t, :n].max()) for t, n, x in zip(pp.task, pp.n_a, pp.x, strict=True)]
rows = []
for n in NS:
    z = pp[(pp.n_a == n) & pp.out]
    b = pd.qcut(z.dA, 4, duplicates="drop")
    g_ = z.groupby([b, "edge"], observed=True).gain.mean().unstack()
    cnt = z.groupby([b, "edge"], observed=True).size().unstack()
    m_ = (g_[False] * cnt[True] / cnt[True].sum()).sum()
    e_ = z[z.edge].gain
    rows.append({"n_A": n, "edge gain": e_.mean(), "edge SE": e_.std() / np.sqrt(len(e_)), "n edge": len(e_),
                 "interior gain, matched": m_, "n interior": int((~z.edge).sum()), "ratio": e_.mean() / m_})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("n_A").round(3))

How to read.

  • First line: the mean |f_A − g| (h = id) at the ends and in the middle of [0, 1], over 4000 prior draws. A leak shows as values near 0 at x = 0 and 1.
  • Table: only queries outside the hull of A's points (where A-only must extrapolate from one side), split into edge and interior, with the interior reweighted to the edge queries' distribution of distance to the nearest A point. A ratio of about 1 = the edge excess is explained by extrapolation.

Here.

  • The prior has no pinning: |f_A − g| is 0.040 at x = 0 and 0.022 at x = 1, against 0.036 in the middle. Notebook 16's leak was 0.003 against 0.055.
  • The matched ratio is 0.93–1.10 at every n_A, with an edge SE of about 0.06.
  • The excess edge gain is A-only extrapolating, not the prior leaking. These controls were added after the results (they are not pre-registered).

How to read.

  • Tables: the NLL at n_A = 3 by the true J, by the number of extrema of g and by h (lower is better).
  • "Share worse than A-only": the fraction of tasks where a method's NLL exceeds A-only's (negative transfer).
  • Runtime: CIS's wall time per task on the GPU, batched 32 tasks at a time.

Here.

  • By J: the transfer methods and the oracle do best at J = 0 (no warp beyond the window) and are similar for J ≥ 2. CIS beats MTPFN in every J stratum, by 0.03–0.06.
  • By extrema:
    • functions with ≥ 3 extrema are hardest for every method (oracle −1.93 against −2.43 for 0 extrema);
    • it is the only stratum where MTPFN beats CIS (by 0.04), and CIS falls 0.05 behind IS-ref there (the C1 coverage failure);
    • this stratum has 20 tasks.
  • By h: with affine h the gains over A-only are smaller for everyone (A's offset and scale must be learned too). CIS keeps a 0.03 lead.
  • Negative transfer: 14–25 % of tasks for MTPFN and CIS, 11–13 % for the oracle. Even exact Bayes is worse than A-only on about 1 task in 9. That is the price of a prior that also allows a B unhelpful for these few points; the learners add about 5–10 points on top.
  • Runtime: CIS-U costs 0.9–3.2 s per task (R = 3, K = 128), against one forward pass for MTPFN.

Reading (pilot, seed 0 for every learned part; the verdict is proposed, not decided)¶

Runs.

  • Decoder: pilot_20261104-174531 (plateau stop at 28 000 steps).
  • MTPFN: pilot_20261104-175731; A-only PFN: pilot_20261104-183902 (100 000 steps each).
  • Evaluation: pilot_20261104-202203 (commit edd69cd, clean). 256 tasks per n_A, all members DONE, none failed.
  • The ablation decoder without the T′ feature (pilot_20261104-201833) finished after the evaluation started, so C8 is not evaluated.

Pre-registered comparison: INCONCLUSIVE.

  • CIS-U (R = 3, K = 128) is better than MTPFN at every n_A, by 0.030 / 0.030 / 0.040 / 0.045 / 0.029 / 0.029 nats at n_A = 1 / 2 / 3 / 5 / 8 / 10.
  • Every paired 95 % CI excludes 0, but no cell reaches the 0.05 margin.
  • CIS is better on 57–66 % of tasks.

The ladder.

  • Share of the A-only → oracle gap closed, from n_A = 1 to 10:
    • MTPFN 80 % → 39 %;
    • CIS 85 % → 54 %;
    • IS-ref 86 % → 60 %.
  • Both learners lose ground as n_A grows. MTPFN's amortisation error (MTPFN − oracle) is 0.12–0.15 nats.

Where CIS's error is. Almost all of it is the decoder, not the proposal.

  • Proposal error (CIS − IS-ref): 0.008–0.017. This passes C3 (≤ 0.03).
  • Decoder error (IS-ref − oracle): 0.081–0.096.
  • With the exact likelihood, the same proposal is within 0.04–0.05 of the oracle at n_A ≤ 8.
  • The teacher (the decoder given the true θ and J) beats the oracle by 0.02–0.22. It conditions on latents the oracle has to infer, so it is not a bound.
  • The next lever is therefore the decoder: it stopped by the plateau rule at 28k steps, and only one seed exists. More proposal work is not the lever.

Hypotheses.

  • C1 fails, and only on the ≥ 3-extrema stratum (20 tasks): hit rate 0.95 / 0.85 / 0.75 at n_A = 5 / 8 / 10. Every other stratum is ≥ 0.94, and most are 1.0.
  • C3 passes.
  • C4 fails: the rounds do not raise the ESS (ratio 1.0–1.1).
  • C5 fails: n_A = 1 is not the hardest case for the proposal.
  • C6 passes: hit rate ≥ 0.96 under affine h.
  • C2 and C1's AIR-flow clause are not evaluated (D4).

p(J) is barely identified. The weight on the true J is 0.21–0.26 for CIS. This is close to the prior, so the complexity posterior adds little here. The oracle's p(J) is calibrated. CIS's is overconfident where it puts more than 0.5 on one J (§5, reliability), either from the decoder's evidence or from weight degeneracy at K = 128 (not separated here).

Calibration. The 90 % coverage is 0.887–0.907 for A-only, MTPFN, CIS and the oracle.

Negative transfer. Share of tasks worse than A-only:

  • MTPFN 14–25 %;
  • CIS 15–24 %;
  • oracle 11–13 %.

Leak audit. The pre-registered audit flags: the ratio is 1.32–2.26. Two post-hoc controls (§7b) attribute it to A-only's one-sided extrapolation at the edge, not to a leak:

  • In the prior, |f_A − g| is 0.022–0.042 at the ends against 0.036 in the middle. Notebook 16's leak was 0.003 against 0.055.
  • Among queries outside A's hull, at a matched distance to the nearest A point, the edge/interior ratio is 0.93–1.10.

Runtime. CIS-U (R = 3, K = 128) takes 0.9–3.2 s per task on the GPU; MTPFN is a single forward pass.

Limits.

  • One training seed for every learned part.
  • The oracle's MC error is 0.014–0.020 nats per task (mean |half 1 − half 2|).
  • The ≥ 3-extrema stratum has 20 tasks.
